title: No Running Lights
passages:
Rain came at the Marrow sideways, and nobody had the deck lights on, because Sol had killed them at dusk to save the batteries and because a boat that shows itself on the drowned coast gets visited. So the deck was lit only by the wheelhouse instruments and the green wash of Wren's slate, which she held in both hands against her chest like a cat she was keeping warm.

The slate did two jobs. Its recorder logged every diver's suit telemetry—depth and air and heart rate—so Wren could sit afterward and rebuild the hours a person lost down there, frame by frame, out of the data their body had kept even when their head hadn't. Its other job was the radar sweep, a thin green line crawling around the screen once every four seconds, pinging anything solid within half a mile and painting it a smudge.

The smudge showed up on the blind side, port quarter, three hundred meters and closing.

"Rusk," Dey said, from where he sat on an upturned crate with his rig open in his lap. He wasn't working on it. There was nothing left to work on; his scrubber cartridge—the canister that pulls carbon dioxide back out of a diver's rebreathed air—was in Teo's chest, and without it Dey could not go below ten meters without poisoning himself. He kept the rig open anyway, the way a man holds his hat in his hands at a burial.

"You can't see anything," Wren said.

"I can't see anything," Dey agreed. "So it's Rusk."

Sol came out of the wheelhouse with a mug she wasn't drinking from. "How close?"

"Two-eighty. Two-sixty." Wren tilted the slate. "He's not lit. No lamp, no masthead, nothing."

"Course?"

"Coming around our stern. Slow. Like a man who's already decided where he's going to stand."

Nia stood in the wheelhouse doorway with her brother behind her, one hand back on Teo's shoulder to keep him in the room. Teo was eleven and had the loose, too-quiet stillness of a kid whose medicine was down to the last few cartridges, and Nia watched the dark the way she watched everything, like it owed her money. "Then he can stay off my boat," she said.

"It's not your boat," Dey said.

"It's not his either."

Wren swept again. Two-ten. She could hear it under the rain now, the low lump of a barge engine running slow, no rhythm to it, no horn. Barge skippers on the coast ran lights because the alternative was another hull through their wheelhouse. This one had the lights off on purpose. That took a kind of confidence Wren didn't like, and it cost nothing, which she liked less.

"He'll hail before we see him," she said.

"Who always hails?"

"Nobody. People who come to take things."

Sol drank nothing from her mug. "Get below, both kids."

"I'm not going below," Nia said.

"Then stand behind me and be quiet, which is a thing you have never once done."

Wren watched the sweep. One-sixty. One-forty. Rain hammered the drum of the winch, the big spool at the bow that pulled divers up, with one good pull left in it if the storm didn't get there first. One-twenty. Still nothing out there to see, only the black and the rain coming through the black. Then the smudge stopped moving, forty meters out, big as a house, and no light anywhere on it.

The voice came across the water before the hull did, close, unhurried, pitched to carry over an engine. A man used to being heard.

"*Marrow.* Heave to. I'm coming along your port side, so don't waste a flare."

Sol set the mug down on the winch housing very carefully, the way you set a thing down when you want your hands free.

"Port side," Dey said. "That's the blind side."

"I know which side it is."

"He was already there," Wren said, and turned the slate around so they could all see the stopped smudge sitting on the screen with nothing to show for it but rain. "Ivo's been calling the backup channel four hundred meters west for two days and nobody's answered him. That's a tower Rusk swears is dead. If that voice is in there, it's the only thing down there still talking, and he's about to tell us so."

He didn't hail twice. The barge came in with one squeal of rubber fender against the Marrow's rail, and before Wren got the sweep around, a hand closed over the top of it from the outside.

Then a knee. Then boots. Then a man standing on her deck.

No line thrown, no hook. He came over the way a man steps over a puddle he's stepped over a hundred times, and then he stood still and let them look. Fifty, maybe past it. Short grey beard trimmed by somebody with a mirror and patience. Dry coat, dry shoulders, dry boots.

That was the part Wren didn't like. Everyone on the drowned coast was wet; it was the condition of the world. This man had crossed forty meters of open black water in the rain and arrived dry, which meant he'd sat out there under a canopy long enough to pick the exact second he wanted to be aboard.

Her slate kept a thin line crawling at the bottom of the screen, deck audio, because a diver's last hour was mostly other people's voices. She was the only one on the boat keeping a record of anything, and she felt it the way you feel a splinter you haven't found yet.

"Anselm Rusk," he said. "I collect for the Factor."

He said it the way other men said their own name. The Factor bought what came up out of the towers and lent against what hadn't come up yet, and when a boat couldn't pay, the Factor sent somebody to take the boat. Rusk was the somebody.

"Sol Ferreira," Sol said. "If you're selling, we're broke. If you're buying, we're broke in a different currency."

"I'm not selling."

"Then congratulations, you're the entertainment. Dey, get the man a mug."

"You didn't ask," Nia said from the wheelhouse door.

"I never do."

Rusk turned a slow half-step so the winch sat at his shoulder and the whole deck lay in front of him, and he laid it out flat. No wind-up, no threat in the voice at all, which was worse than a threat.

"There was a cold-case out of Mercy General. Sealed, dry, worth twelve thousand to the Factor's buyer upcoast. It isn't in your hold and it isn't on your deck, so it's in the water. You've got until the storm turns to bring it up and put it in my hands."

"Says who."

"Says the glass in my wheelhouse and the glass in yours." He tipped his chin north, where there was nothing to see yet. "Wind swings round at first light. Then this mooring is a reef. When it turns, I come alongside and I take the case's value or I take the Marrow. Your pick, Captain. Either one clears what's owed."

"And if I pick neither?"

"Then I take the boat, and you people are in the water with a storm coming in." He said it without heat, the way you'd read out a tide table. "I've only had to do that twice. Both times it was cheaper than arguing."

Dey had come up off his crate with the open rig still hanging from one hand. "You'd put a kid in the water."

"I'd put everybody in the water. It's less work than sorting."

"One day," Sol said.

"One day." Rusk glanced at the winch drum, at the coil of spliced line, at the deck lights that weren't on. "If you've got a pocket still down there, Captain, you'd want to start now instead of standing here being clever at me."

Wren watched the rain come off the drum and thought about the number. Twelve thousand bought berths on the high ground, four of them, above the storm line, and Sol had had it in her hands and let it go down in the dark. Sol, standing there with her mug of nothing, looked like a woman who'd had a good sleep.

Rusk looked at her too. Longer than he'd looked at anything else on the boat. Wren saw him file it, whatever it was, and then he started walking, slow, unhurried, a man reading a room he already owned.

Rusk stopped three feet from Sol, close enough that she could smell him—dry wool and something sharp, like ozone left in a tin too long. He didn't look at the winch anymore. He looked at her face.

"You look peaceful, Captain," he said. "Too peaceful for a woman who just lost twelve thousand in the dark."

Sol lifted her mug. "I never had it."

"The cold-case came up. I know it came up. Your slate says you were on the winch when it went back down." He kept his voice flat. "And then you came up with nothing. Not a dent in the drum, not a mark on your hands, and an hour missing from the recorder that only your reader can fix."

"I was tired," Sol said. "I slept through it."

"Convenient." Rusk glanced at the wheelhouse door, where Nia stood with her arms crossed and Teo tucked behind her like a secret. "Or it's a bluff. You took the case, you hid it, and now you're hoping I'll believe you don't remember so I'll go easy on you. I don't go easy. That's how you end up in the water."

"I don't remember," Sol said, and her voice was quiet but not shaken. She really didn't. "If I had twelve thousand, I'd buy my berths and you'd be on your barge already."

"Then you're bluffing about the hour, or you're bluffing about the case. Either way, I call it." Rusk turned his head toward Nia. "You, by the door. You look like you remember everything."

Nia didn't move. "I remember you're standing on a boat that isn't yours."

Rusk smiled. It didn't reach his eyes. "Spirited. The girl in the tower. I heard you sealed the case yourself."

"I heard you're a debt collector with a dry coat in a rainstorm," Nia said. "Get off my deck."

"Your deck." Rusk looked past her to Wren, who hadn't moved from her spot by the winch housing, slate still clutched to her chest. "And you. The reader. You know what's in that missing hour better than she does, don't you?"

Wren said nothing. She looked at the green wash of her screen, at the thin line of deck audio crawling at the bottom, and said nothing. Her own edit sat in there, clean and quiet, and she had never told Sol a word of it.

Rusk took another step, this one toward the cold-box lashed behind the wheelhouse. Dey moved. He didn't say anything; he just stepped between Rusk and the box, the open rig hanging from his hand like a dropped weapon.

"Now that's loyalty," Rusk said. "Or guilt. You gave your scrubber to the kid. Can't go below ten meters without turning blue, and you're still standing in front of his medicine."

"He's not diving," Dey said. "And neither are you."

Rusk looked down at the rig, then back up at Dey's face. "You're not much of a threat without air."

"I don't need air to break your fingers," Dey said.

Rusk held his gaze for a beat, then let his eyes slide past Dey to the cold-box. "Medicine cartridges. Spare scrubbers. The boy's course runs on them, I'd guess." He smiled again, thinner this time. "Interesting what you people keep on deck instead of in the hold."

He reached out. His fingers found the latch. Dey didn't move, and Nia didn't move, and Wren kept staring at her slate like the answer was written there in green light. The rain came down harder, drumming on the roof of the wheelhouse, and the latch gave under Rusk's thumb with a small metallic click.

The inside of the cold-box was somebody's idea of order. Blue gel packs cut to fit the walls. A cardboard tray, and a strip of tape across the tray with a name on it in marker: TEO. Beside the name, tally marks. Nine of them, and beside the ninth an empty slot the width of a thumb.

Rusk read the tape the way he'd read everything on the boat, like a price. Then he reached in past Dey's shoulder, unhurried, a man taking a mint off a table, and lifted out three of the four cartridges standing in the tray. Glass, a thumb long, a blue crimp seal at one end. You snapped the crimp and breathed through it for ten minutes and the drug went down into the wet parts of a kid's chest and told them to stop filling. Without it Teo's breathing went shallow and fast, and then it didn't go at all. Ten days to a course. Nine marks on the tape.

Rusk put three of them in the inside pocket of the dry coat.

"The last one's not yours," Wren said.

"None of it's yours." He pressed the pocket flat with his palm. "Call it earnest. Good faith. You hand me twelve thousand at first light, I hand these back and we're friends."

"We don't have twelve thousand," Dey said.

"Then we're not going to be friends."

Sol hadn't moved off the winch housing. "You're robbing a sick kid on my deck in front of witnesses."

"Four witnesses." Rusk didn't look at her. "Five, if the boy's old enough to talk."

Nia came off the doorframe without a sound, which was the frightening part. She didn't go for his face. She went low and fast for the pocket, both hands, the way you go for something floating away from you in cold water.

Rusk laughed and turned his hip and let her have the coat. The seam gave with a small dry rip. Then he put a hand flat on her sternum and shoved, and she went down on the wet planks hard enough that the whole boat heard it, and the fourth cartridge jumped out of the torn pocket and spun away across the deck.

Dey's boot came down over it. He didn't look down at it.

"Keep that one," Rusk said. "I'm not walking back for it."

"You put a kid on the deck," Sol said.

"She put herself there. I've been assaulted by worse and drier." He straightened the coat, found the rip with two fingers, and seemed pleased with the arithmetic of it. "One day left on that course, by my count. Generous of me, because the storm turns before then, and after that it's water in the box and water in the boy."

Nia sat up. Her lip was split and she didn't bother with it. "You came out here in a boat with no lights to steal a cartridge off a child."

"I came out here to see what you'd fight for." Rusk looked around the deck, at the winch, at the spliced line, at Sol's face, and filed it all somewhere behind his eyes. "Now I know. Good. Makes the morning simpler."

He walked. Not fast. Past the wheelhouse, toward his rail, hands in his pockets like a man leaving a shop.

Nobody moved until he was three steps gone. Then Wren said, "Nine marks. He left one."

"I can count," Nia said, from the deck.

Teo had come out of the wheelhouse to stand in the rain in his socks. He looked at the tape, at the one empty slot, and said, "I'm fine," and nobody looked at him, which was the kindest thing available.

Wren turned the slate around. The line at the bottom was still crawling, deck audio, every voice on the boat for the last two hours laid down in green, including a man saying *call it earnest* in a dry coat. She could cut that. She had cut worse. Her thumb found the wheel and stopped there.

"Somebody's going down to that pocket tonight," Nia said, getting up. "And it isn't going to be you, reader. There's no rig on this boat that'll take you past thirty."

"I know what's on this boat," Wren said, and put the slate against her chest.

The wheelhouse speaker spat static, a dry crackle that cut through the rain on the roof. Everyone turned.

A man's voice, thin with pressure and distance, came through the backup channel: "*Tell the kid... keep going. Tell her... Wren... tell Wren Achebe...*"

The name hung in the wet air. Wren felt her throat close. She had never given that name to a diver at forty-two meters. She had never given it to anyone down there.

Rusk stopped at his rail. His hands came out of his pockets slow, like he was being measured. He looked at the wheelhouse window, then at Wren, then back at the black water alongside the hull.

"That tower's dead," he said. "I signed the survey myself. Nothing lives at forty-two in Mercy General. Nothing *talks*."

The speaker hissed again. "*...keep going... tell her I... I sealed them... I sealed the case...*"

Nia was on her feet, one hand on the doorframe. "That's the hospital tower. That's where we came from."

"Was," Rusk said. "Past tense. I dove that shaft two years ago. Collapsed at thirty-eight. I lost a man checking it. There is no forty-two."

"Then who's talking?" Dey asked.

Rusk didn't answer. He stared at the speaker grille like it had bitten him. The rain drummed on the wheelhouse roof. The slate in Wren's hands kept crawling its green line, deck audio recording everything, and the voice on the backup channel kept breathing, slow and ragged, like a man who had been waiting a long time for someone to listen.

"*Wren,*" the voice said again. "*You swore. You swore you'd bring the winch.*"

Wren's thumb pressed the edit wheel. She didn't turn it. She couldn't decide what to cut.
